- Filtering is the process of altering the spectrum of a signal. A filter can remove or attenuate specific frequencies, and/or boost others.

- Filtering is the process of altering the spectrum of a signal. A filter can remove or attenuate specific frequencies, and/or boost others. 
- In this first example, we use a lowpass filter to cut-off all frequencies above the one specified with the slider.
- Inversely, we can use a highpass filter to filter out frequencies below a certain threshold.

:::

## Faust: Filtering {auto-animate=true}
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

:::: {.columns .faust-layout}
::: {.column width="50%" .add-space}
::: {style="font-size: 90%;"}
::: {style="opacity: 0.5"}
- Filtering is the process of altering the spectrum of a signal. A filter can remove or attenuate specific frequencies, and/or boost others. 
- In this first example, we use a lowpass filter to cut-off all frequencies above the one specified with the slider.
- Inversely, we can use a highpass filter to filter out frequencies below a certain threshold.
- ... or specify a restrictive frequency band, using a bandpass filter.
:::
- In general, filters are applied progressively, the frequency decay (rolloff) depends on the filter order.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="44%"}

## Faust: Filtering {auto-animate=true}
<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

:::: {.columns .faust-layout}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="font-size: 90%;"}
::: {style="opacity: 0.5"}
- Filtering is the process of altering the spectrum of a signal. A filter can remove or attenuate specific frequencies, and/or boost others. 
- In this first example, we use a lowpass filter to cut-off all frequencies above the one specified with the slider.
- Inversely, we can use a highpass filter to filter out frequencies below a certain threshold.
- ... or specify a restrictive frequency band, using a bandpass filter.
:::
- In general, filters are applied progressively, the frequency decay (rolloff) depends on the filter order.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.content style="padding-left: 5%; width: 110%;"}
```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np;
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt;
from scipy import signal;

fs = 48000;

b1, a1 = signal.butter(1, 1000, btype='low', fs=fs);
b2, a2 = signal.butter(2, 1000, btype='low', fs=fs);
b4, a4 = signal.butter(4, 1000, btype='low', fs=fs);
b8, a8 = signal.butter(8, 1000, btype='low', fs=fs);
w1, h1 = signal.freqz(b1, a1, fs=fs);
w2, h2 = signal.freqz(b2, a2, fs=fs);
w4, h4 = signal.freqz(b4, a4, fs=fs);
w8, h8 = signal.freqz(b8, a8, fs=fs);

# Filter frequency response:
plt.figure(facecolor="#fdf6e3")
ax = plt.gca()
ax.set_facecolor("#fdf6e3")
plt.grid();
plt.plot(w1, 20 * np.log10(np.abs(h1)), label="Order 1");
plt.plot(w2, 20 * np.log10(np.abs(h2)), label="Order 2");
plt.plot(w4, 20 * np.log10(np.abs(h4)), label="Order 4");
plt.plot(w8, 20 * np.log10(np.abs(h8)), label="Order 8");
plt.xlabel("Frequency (Hz)");
plt.ylabel("Magnitude (dB)");
plt.title("Butterworth filter frequency response");
plt.legend();
plt.show();
```
:::
